title: Cancer-induced nerve injury promotes resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy
one_line: The paper reports that nerve injury caused by tumour invasion drives resistance to anti-PD-1 checkpoint blockade, linking cancer neuroscience to immunotherapy failure.
key_claims: Cancer-induced injury to peripheral nerves within or near the tumour is associated with reduced response to anti-PD-1 therapy.
The authors frame nerve injury, rather than nerve presence alone, as the feature that promotes an immunotherapy-resistant state.
Targeting the nerve-injury axis is proposed as a route to restore checkpoint blockade sensitivity.
No specific effect sizes, cohort sizes, or model details were provided in the episode's show notes.
limitations: The show notes contain only the DOI, so the specific tumour types, models, and quantitative results underlying the claims are not recorded here.
Authors' own stated limitations were not captured in the available material.
Whether the nerve-injury-to-resistance link is causal in humans versus correlative in patient samples is not established from the material given.
open_questions: Does experimentally preventing or reversing cancer-induced nerve injury restore anti-PD-1 response in vivo?
Is a nerve-injury signature predictive of checkpoint blockade outcome in independent patient cohorts?
Which immune cell populations mediate the resistance downstream of the injured nerve?
